groups.title: Persian sayings
groups.q: These Persian sayings are translated word for word. Try to guess each one first, then show its meaning.

rows.text: Rain doesn't fall upward from the earth.
rows.note: Some things only go one way and never happen in reverse. Here: parents sacrifice for their children, not children for their parents.

rows.text: A good year is known from its spring.
rows.note: A good start shows how things will turn out.

rows.text: Don't eat sorrow
rows.note: Don't be sad; don't worry.

rows.text: my heart is rotting
rows.note: I'm bored to death; waiting or loneliness is wearing me down.

rows.text: My hand is short and union with you is far.
rows.note: What I want is out of my reach; I'm powerless. Here: being with you.

rows.text: if I say it, my tongue burns; if I don't say it, the marrow of my bones burns
rows.note: A painful choice: speaking hurts, but keeping quiet hurts more.

rows.text: the meal will turn to snake venom for me
rows.note: Something good gets spoiled, so I can't enjoy it. Here: he'll ruin the meal for me.

rows.text: no bread is going to warm up for you
rows.note: You'll gain nothing from it; it's pointless.

rows.text: my family shoved me into the henhouse
rows.note: A joking way to say "to get married". Here: my family pushed me into marriage.

rows.text: the sugar cube jumps in my throat
rows.note: It goes down the wrong way and I choke. In Iran, tea is often drunk through a sugar cube held in the mouth.

rows.text: peek into every last corner
rows.note: Explore everywhere; look into everything out of curiosity.

rows.text: words cost nothing; it's just hot air
rows.note: Talk is cheap; words alone prove nothing.

rows.text: he would surely fall from Negar's eyes
rows.note: To lose someone's respect. Here: the girl would stop thinking well of him.

rows.text: Just a harvest-time promise?
rows.note: A promise for a "later" that never comes; an empty promise.

rows.text: let me serve you the guts of friendship on a tray
rows.note: To offer someone your whole heart. Here: all my friendship.

rows.text: all their body hair fell right out
rows.note: To be completely stunned.

rows.text: don't get so worked up, or your milk will dry up
rows.note: Getting too angry will harm you (first said to nursing mothers). Here: calm down, it isn't worth it.

rows.text: no one will call you mute if you don't fart
rows.note: A crude form of "nobody calls you mute if you don't speak": you could just keep quiet. Here: nobody would have minded if you'd kept quiet.

rows.text: Eat the head of my dick
rows.note: A very rude "get lost": nobody cares what you think.

rows.text: You dick-head eater
rows.note: A crude insult, roughly "you idiot", often between friends.

rows.text: laughing at our beards and dicks
rows.note: To mock someone (from "laughing at someone's beard", made crude). Here: making fun of us who stayed behind.

rows.text: wandering the streets like this with your dick in your hand
rows.note: Idle and aimless, with nothing to show for it. Here: still single, wandering around alone.

rows.text: no matter what dick lands on our heads
rows.note: Whatever disaster hits us (crude).

rows.text: they've rammed a pole up the ass of every one of us from the provinces
rows.note: To treat someone very unfairly (crude). Here: the policy did that to all of us from the provinces.

rows.text: You couldn't even eat its head.
rows.note: A rude reply: you couldn't have done a thing ("its head" = the head of a dick).

rows.text: I could go round and round my Nini-jan's head.
rows.note: A loving phrase: I'd take your troubles on myself (from an old custom of circling a loved one to keep misfortune away). Here: I'd give anything for her.

groups.title: Children's words
groups.q: Some children in the book get words wrong, the way small children do. Does each one sound like a child's mistake, not a typo?

rows.text: It's marmal stone. Marmal means really expensive.
rows.note: marmal = marble

rows.text: It's called Tatanic.
rows.note: Tatanic = Titanic

rows.text: Baba, Baba, wiw you buy me dis big dolly?
rows.note: a little girl

rows.text: Yes, I wiw buy you a dolly.
rows.note: her father copies her

groups.title: Nicknames
groups.q: The friends in the book give each other playful nicknames, often as wordplay. Does each one work as a nickname in your language?

rows.text: Alain Dickon
rows.note: a nickname for one of the friends: the actor Alain Delon's name, with part of it turned into a rude word for penis

rows.text: Elder of the Tavern
rows.note: a mock-grand title, taken from Hafez's poetry

rows.text: Eldie
rows.note: a pet form of "Elder of the Tavern"

rows.text: Taverny, my Tavvy
rows.note: pet forms made from "tavern"

rows.text: Leopard Farid
rows.note: for a daring, reckless friend

rows.text: Is Arasteh a trimmed-down Araasteh?
rows.note: araasteh = Persian for "neat"

rows.text: Her Ladyship Ms. Armaaan
rows.note: the surname Arman, drawn out to mock

rows.text: Mister Curly-haired Schrödinger
rows.note: a mock title for someone who can't make up his mind

groups.title: A line by Hafez
groups.q: This line by the poet Hafez is written without a comma, so it can be read in two opposite ways:

rows.text: The wine there is real no metaphor.

after: One way: the wine is real, not a metaphor.
The other way: the wine is not real, only a metaphor.
groups.after_q: Can your version be read both ways?
